Neonatal body mass in Verreaux's sifaka (Propithecus verreauxi) is surprisingly modest given the species' adult dimensions, with newborns weighing approximately 72.25 grams [Wwb = approximately 72.25 grams]. This relatively small birth mass is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes extended maternal investment over rapid early growth, a pattern observed among several lemurids. During the suckling period, the milk-dependent young undergoes a dramatic transformation, nearly doubling in mass before reaching the weaning milestone. Under a stable core temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], nutritional independence is achieved at 150 days after birth [tx = 150 days after birth]. At this point, the offspring, now nutritionally independent, weighs in the range of 1000 grams [Wwx = 1000 grams], representing a substantial gain from its birth weight. The transition to a solid-food diet is gradual, with the juvenile continuing to associate closely with its mother while increasing its intake of leaves, fruits, and flowers over several subsequent weeks. This prolonged period of maternal dependence is thought to facilitate social learning of complex foraging techniques, a critical skill in the seasonally dry forests of Madagascar.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Verreaux's sifaka averages approximately 5000 grams [Wwi = approximately 5000 grams], placing them among the medium-sized members of the family Indriidae. This adult body mass is achieved through a slow and steady growth trajectory, with individuals not reaching full size until several years after weaning. Considerable variation exists within populations, with some adults recorded weighing between 3000 grams and 7000 grams, reflecting differences in habitat quality, sex, and individual condition. Males and females are similar in body size, though females may experience slight mass fluctuations during gestation and lactation. The relatively modest adult mass compared to that of the related indri (Indri indri) is likely an adaptation to the more seasonal and unpredictable resource availability in the dry forests and spiny thickets of southern and southwestern Madagascar. This body size influences a range of physiological parameters, including metabolic rate, home range requirements, and social dynamics within the multi-male, multi-female groups typical of the species.

Basal metabolic rate measurements obtained via respirometry under controlled laboratory conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] have established the maximum resting oxygen consumption for Verreaux's sifaka at 670 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 670 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate is consistent with the low energy expenditure typical of folivorous primates, reflecting a diet dominated by leaves that are often high in fiber and low in readily available calories. The measured oxygen consumption at this stable core temperature provides a valuable baseline for understanding the species' energetic constraints, particularly during the cool, dry winter months when food quality declines. Energy budgeting studies suggest that this moderate metabolic demand allows the sifaka to subsist on a relatively low-quality diet while maintaining the social cohesion of its group, as extensive daily ranging for scarce high-quality food items is not required. Comparative data from other folivorous lemurs indicate that this metabolic rate is near the lower end of the predicted range for a primate of this body size, highlighting an energy-saving strategy that may be crucial for surviving extended periods of resource scarcity.

Gestation in Verreaux's sifaka is completed in approximately 148 days [tg = approximately 148 days] when measured at a maternal core body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that places this species within the typical range for lemurs of its body size. This period of embryogenesis and foetal development is characterized by relatively slow foetal growth, a pattern linked to the overall slow life history of the species. Following a single live birth, the eutherian foetus emerges as a precocial neonate, already furred and with eyes open, able to cling to the mother's belly within hours of parturition. The reproductive output of this species is extremely low, with females typically producing a single offspring per year, corresponding to a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 1 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 1 offspring per year]. This low fecundity, combined with the relatively long gestation, underscores the considerable maternal investment required for each newborn and explains the vulnerability of populations to any increase in adult mortality, whether from habitat fragmentation or predation.

The lifespan of Verreaux's sifaka in the wild reaches approximately 31 years [am = approximately 31 years] when considering individuals living under the stable thermal conditions of a typical 36 °C [T = 36 °C] core body temperature. This remarkable longevity is among the longest documented for any lemur of equivalent body size and reflects the extremely slow pace of life characteristic of this clade. Sexual maturation, marking the onset of reproductive viability, is a delayed process, with puberty occurring at 912 days after birth [tp = 912 days after birth] under the same thermoregulatory regime of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This prolonged juvenile and sub-adult period represents a significant time investment in somatic development before any reproductive effort is initiated. The time between the achievement of sexual maturity and first successful reproduction may extend further, as social dynamics within the group — including dominance hierarchies and access to mates — often delay actual breeding beyond the point of physiological readiness. This constellation of late maturity, long gestation, single-offspring births, and extended lifespan places Propithecus verreauxi squarely at the slow end of the primate life-history continuum.
